demoMeetings.title: A calmer home for your meetings
demoMeetings.summary: The team explored a simpler way to organise recordings in Jottie. The direction is a familiar three-pane workspace: folders for context, a scannable meeting list, and a focused space to read. The first prototype will prioritise finding and revisiting conversations.
highlights: Keep folders visible while moving between meetings, so you never lose your place.
Use the meeting summary as the list preview, with dates, duration and a few useful tags.
Give the summary and transcript their own views, with a shared meeting header.
decisions: Move forward with a three-pane layout for the desktop experience.
Open meetings on the summary, with the transcript one click away.

actions.task: Explore the folder tree and meeting list together
Review the prototype with a small set of sample recordings
Map the agreed component structure to the macOS app

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: Let’s start with what happens after a meeting. You have a recording, but the useful part is being able to come back and find that one decision a week later.

transcript.speaker: Jamie Chen
transcript.text: I think the folder tree should stay with you. Then the next column can work like an inbox: a title, a date and enough of the summary to recognise the conversation.

transcript.speaker: Sam Ellis
transcript.text: That maps quite nicely to the desktop app. We can give each pane its own scroll area, so reading a long transcript doesn’t move your meeting list.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: Exactly. Let’s make the default view a summary. I want to see the main points, what we decided and what needs to happen next.

transcript.speaker: Jamie Chen
transcript.text: And the transcript is one tab away. We don’t need to put everything on the screen at once. A bit of breathing room will make this much easier to read.

transcript.speaker: Sam Ellis
transcript.text: Let’s use sample meetings for the first pass. Once the layout feels right, we can map the component structure back to the native app.

demoMeetings.title: Design review: small details, less friction
demoMeetings.summary: A review of navigation, selected states and reading comfort. We agreed to keep the interface quiet and let the meeting content do most of the talking.
highlights: Selected meetings need a clear, quiet highlight.
Use one accent colour consistently for navigation and primary actions.
decisions: Keep the toolbar compact and use labelled tabs for content views.

actions.task: Check the layout in both light and dark mode

transcript.speaker: Jamie Chen
transcript.text: The structure is working. I’d like to focus on the little things now: selected states, spacing and how comfortable a long summary is to read.

transcript.speaker: Sam Ellis
transcript.text: Let’s keep one clear accent colour. The rest can be neutral so that the content stays the focus.

demoMeetings.title: What makes a meeting worth revisiting?
demoMeetings.summary: Research planning around how people return to past conversations. Finding decisions and remembering context emerged as the two most useful starting points.
highlights: People often remember the project before they remember the meeting title.
A short preview helps people recognise the right conversation.
decisions: Test folder navigation alongside a search across meeting text.

actions.task: Draft five tasks for the next usability session

transcript.speaker: Robin Taylor
transcript.text: When people look back, they’re usually asking what we decided, or why. We should build our research tasks around those questions.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: And let’s check how they find the meeting in the first place. I suspect project folders and a useful preview will both matter.

demoMeetings.title: Website direction & first impressions
demoMeetings.summary: The website should show the product in use and explain its value in a few clear sentences. A real product view will lead the homepage.
highlights: Lead with the experience of finding useful moments in past meetings.
Keep the first page focused on one clear story.
decisions: Use a product screenshot as the main visual.

transcript.speaker: Jamie Chen
transcript.text: The homepage should show the workspace straight away. People should be able to picture how it fits into their day.

transcript.speaker: Robin Taylor
transcript.text: Agreed. One clear story and a useful product image will go further than a long feature list.

demoMeetings.title: A clearer story for the homepage
demoMeetings.summary: A short working session on the homepage narrative, from capturing a conversation to finding the useful parts later.
highlights: Explain the value through a familiar everyday task.
decisions: Write the first draft around revisiting decisions.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: Let’s tell the story from the moment someone needs to remember a decision. That gives the product a clear purpose.

demoMeetings.title: A little detour through Hyrule
demoMeetings.summary: A personal voice note about exploration in Zelda, favourite soundtracks and the pleasure of discovering something without a map marker.
highlights: The best discoveries often happen when the game leaves room for curiosity.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: I’ve been thinking about why exploring Hyrule feels so good. There’s always something just over the next hill, and the game trusts you to go and look.

demoMeetings.title: An idea on the walk home
demoMeetings.summary: A quick thought about giving each project folder a short overview of its recent conversations and open questions.
highlights: A folder overview could help reconnect the threads between conversations.

actions.task: Sketch what a folder overview might contain

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: What if opening a project folder gave you a little context before the meeting list? Just the recent decisions and the questions we haven’t answered yet.

demoMeetings.title: Monday morning thoughts
demoMeetings.summary: A few thoughts for the week: finish the workspace prototype, leave time for a design review and keep the first version focused.
highlights: A small, complete experience is easier to evaluate than a wide collection of unfinished screens.
decisions: Review the workspace before adding more features.

transcript.speaker: Alex Morgan
transcript.text: This week I want to get the workspace into a shape we can click around in. The goal is to understand the layout before we start connecting anything.
